title: Jaipur
selection: Rajasthan recorded 2.07 million foreign tourist visits in 2024, fifth among states (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025, Table 4.1.2). Jaipur is the state capital and the third point of the Delhi–Agra–Jaipur Golden Triangle; it holds two UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Jantar Mantar and Amber Fort, part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan) and the walled city is itself a World Heritage City.

JP1.topic: Founded in 1727 by Jai Singh II
JP1.claim: Jaipur was founded in 1727 by the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler Jai Singh II, who named it after himself; it is believed to be India's first planned city of the Common Era.

evidence.quote: It was established in 1727 by Kachhwaha Rajput ruler Jai Singh II, who named it after himself.

JP2.topic: Why the Pink City is pink
JP2.claim: The city was painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales, giving Jaipur its name 'Pink City'.

evidence.quote: the city was painted pink to welcome Albert Edward, Prince of Wales in 1876
In 1876, to welcome the Prince of Wales, Maharaja Ram Singh of Jaipur had the entire city painted pink, as the colour symbolised hospitality.

JP3.claim: Jaipur was named to UNESCO's World Heritage list as a city on 6 July 2019.

evidence.quote: On 6 July 2019, the city was named to the World Heritage Cities list.

JP4.claim: Jaipur is one of the three points of the Golden Triangle with Delhi and Agra.

evidence.quote: is one of the three points of the Golden Triangle, which comprises Delhi, Agra, and Jaipur

JP5.claim: Jaipur is about 268 km from New Delhi and 232 km from Agra by road; the Ministry of Tourism puts the drive from Delhi at about 5 hours.

evidence.quote: Located 268 km (167 miles) from the national capital New Delhi
Jaipur - 232 km

JP6.claim: Jaipur has direct trains to major cities, including the Shatabdi and Rajdhani to Delhi.

evidence.quote: Jaipur Railway Station offers direct trains to major cities, including Delhi via Shatabdi, Rajdhani, Duronto, and Mandor Express.

JP7.claim: Jaipur International Airport is at Sanganer, about 10 km south of the city centre.

evidence.quote: It is located in the southern suburb of Sanganer , located about 10 km (6.2 mi) from the city centre.

JP8.claim: The Jaipur Metro's Pink Line runs east–west between Mansarovar and Badi Chaupar in the old city.

evidence.quote: Phase 1 of the Jaipur Metro project comprises the East–West Corridor between Mansarovar and Badi Chaupar

JP9.claim: Jaipur has long, extremely hot summers and short, mild winters; most rain falls in July and August.

evidence.quote: with long, extremely hot summers and short mild to warm winters

JP10.claim: Must-try dishes include dal baati churma, kachori, mirchi bada, ker sangri and, for non-vegetarians, laal maas.

evidence.quote: Some of the must-try dishes in Jaipur include the iconic Dal Bati Churma

JP14.claim: Jaipur's festivals include Gangaur, the Jaipur Literature Festival, the Kite Festival and Teej.

evidence.quote: Incredible India Tourist Infoline 1800-11-1363

AH1.claim: Commissioned in 1868 to designs by Samuel Swinton Jacob, the Albert Hall Museum opened to the public in 1887.

JL1.claim: Jal Mahal stands in Man Sagar Lake; most of the building is under water, with only the top floor showing.

most of the building rests submerged beneath the lake's surface, with only the top floor visible.

evidence.quote: Galtaji is situated in the Aravalli Hills, about 10 km east of Jaipur, Rajasthan.

GG1.claim: Garh Ganesh sits on an Aravalli hilltop reached by about 365 steps, with wide views over Jaipur.

evidence.quote: Cultural Heritage Conservation Award in 2000

JB1.claim: Johari Bazaar is known for jewellery, clothes and textiles; Rajasthali, the government showroom on MI Road, and Nehru, Bapu and Tripolia bazaars are the other main shopping streets.

places.name: Jaipur
places.summary: Rajasthan's Pink City: Amber Fort, Hawa Mahal, the City Palace and Jantar Mantar, bazaars full of block prints and gems — the third point of the Golden Triangle.
places.seoTitle: Jaipur Travel Guide: Amber Fort, Hawa Mahal & City Palace
places.seoDescription: Plan your Jaipur trip: Amber Fort, Hawa Mahal, City Palace and Jantar Mantar timings, getting there from Delhi and Agra, bazaars, food and a 2-day itinerary.

images.alt: The pink, honeycomb facade of Hawa Mahal with its hundreds of small windows in Jaipur
images.caption: Hawa Mahal, Jaipur

overview.text:
Jaipur was founded in 1727 by Jai Singh II, who named it after himself, and was laid out as one of India's earliest planned cities. Its old city earned the name 'Pink City' in 1876, when it was painted pink to welcome the Prince of Wales, and in 2019 the walled city was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list.

The capital of Rajasthan, Jaipur is the third point of the Golden Triangle with Delhi and Agra. Its sights fall into two groups. In the old city, Hawa Mahal, the City Palace and the Jantar Mantar observatory — another World Heritage Site — are within a few minutes of each other. About 11 km north, Amber Fort and Jaigarh Fort crown the hills above Maota Lake, with Nahargarh on the ridge in between.

Two days covers the essentials: one for Amber and the hill forts, one for the old city and its bazaars. Note that the markets generally close on Sundays.

items.body: Amber Fort: the 16th-century hill palace with its mirror-covered Sheesh Mahal.
Hawa Mahal: 953 latticed windows on a five-storey facade, built in 1799.
City Palace: still home to Jaipur's royal family, with a museum of royal collections.
Jantar Mantar: 18th-century astronomical instruments, including the world's largest stone sundial.
Nahargarh at sunset: the whole city spread out below the ridge.

best_time.text: Jaipur has long, extremely hot summers and short, mild winters, so the cooler months are by far the most comfortable for climbing forts and walking the bazaars. Most rain falls in July and August. The city's festival calendar is a good reason to time a visit: the Jaipur Literature Festival, the Kite Festival, Gangaur and Teej all draw crowds.

how_to_reach.text:
By road, Jaipur is about 268 km from New Delhi — the Ministry of Tourism puts the drive at about 5 hours — and 232 km from Agra, which makes it the natural last stop of a Golden Triangle trip. Direct trains, including the Shatabdi and Rajdhani, link Jaipur station with Delhi; book on IRCTC.

Jaipur International Airport is at Sanganer, about 10 km south of the centre.

local_transport.text: The Jaipur Metro's Pink Line runs east–west from Mansarovar to Badi Chaupar in the old city, useful for reaching the bazaar area. For Amber, Jaigarh and Nahargarh in the hills, hire a taxi or auto-rickshaw for the half day — agree the fare and waiting time in advance.

where_to_stay.text: Staying in or near the walled old city puts Hawa Mahal, the City Palace and the bazaars within walking distance, though streets are busy and noisy. Quieter areas with more space lie outside the walls to the south and west. Amber is a short drive north whichever you choose.

items.body: Dal baati churma: lentils, baked wheat dumplings and sweet crumbled wheat — Rajasthan's signature dish.
Snacks: kachori and mirchi bada (chilli fritters).
Laal maas, a fiery red mutton curry, for non-vegetarians.
Masala Chowk at Ram Niwas Bagh, which brings Jaipur's street food together in one place.
Shop Johari Bazaar for jewellery and textiles and Bapu Bazaar for mojari shoes — but not on a Sunday, when most markets close.
Look for Sanganeri, Bagru and Dabu block-printed textiles.
Watch the sound and light show at Amber Fort in the evening.
See the Jaivana cannon at Jaigarh Fort.
Dress modestly at temples and remove your shoes where asked.
Bargaining is normal in the bazaars; fixed-price government emporiums are an alternative.
Ask before photographing people.

items.title: Visas
items.body: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days before arrival; your passport needs at least six months' validity.

items.title: Payments
items.body: Visitors can pay by QR code with NPCI's UPI One World wallet after a passport-and-visa KYC check. Carry cash for markets and rickshaws.

items.title: Monument tickets
items.body: Check current fees on the Government of Rajasthan's official tourism and ticketing sites before you go.

items.title: Sundays
items.body: Bazaars are generally closed — plan forts and museums for Sunday.

items.title: Emergency
items.body: Dial 112 for police, fire or ambulance. The Incredible India tourist infoline is 1800-11-1363.

items.title: Heat
items.body: Summers are extremely hot — start early, carry water and rest at midday.

items.title: Steep paths
items.body: The climbs to Amber and Jaigarh are steep and uneven; wear sturdy shoes.

items.title: How many days do I need in Jaipur?
items.body: Two days: one for Amber, Jaigarh and Nahargarh, and one for the old city — Hawa Mahal, the City Palace and Jantar Mantar.

items.title: How far is Jaipur from Delhi and Agra?
items.body: About 268 km from Delhi (around 5 hours by road) and 232 km from Agra.

items.title: Why is Jaipur called the Pink City?
items.body: The city was painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales.

items.title: Can I visit Jal Mahal?
items.body: Not inside — it is no longer open to tourists — but you can see it from the lakeside and from Nahargarh.
Do Amber Fort first thing in the morning, before the heat and the tour buses.
Group the old-city sights: Hawa Mahal, Jantar Mantar and the City Palace are minutes apart.
Save Nahargarh for sunset.

places.name: Amber Fort
places.summary: The hilltop palace of the Kachhwaha kings above Maota Lake, built from 1592 — a UNESCO-listed hill fort with a dazzling mirror palace.
places.seoTitle: Amber Fort Jaipur: Timings, Sheesh Mahal & Light Show
places.seoDescription: Visit Amber (Amer) Fort near Jaipur: opening hours, the route through Jaleb Chowk to the Sheesh Mahal, the evening sound and light show and the tunnel to Jaigarh.

images.alt: Amber Fort's sandstone walls and palace on the hillside above Maota Lake under a blue sky
images.caption: Amber Fort above Maota Lake

images.alt: The illuminated Ganesh Pol gateway of Amber Palace at night

overview.text:
Amber — also spelt Amer — sits on a hill about 11 km from central Jaipur, looking down over Maota Lake. Raja Man Singh I began the palace in 1592, and it was the seat of the Kachhwaha rulers until they moved their capital down to the plains and founded Jaipur. In 2013 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site as one of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

The visit climbs through the Suraj Pol gate into Jaleb Chowk, the old parade ground, then on to the Diwan-e-Aam, the hall of public audience. The highlight is the Sheesh Mahal, a palace of mirrors whose walls and ceilings are covered in tiny pieces of glass. Underground tunnels, partly restored, link Amber with Jaigarh Fort on the hill above. In the evening the fort hosts a sound and light show.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9 am – 6 pm.

items.title: Sound and light show
items.body: Evenings, in English and Hindi; start times vary by season (6:30 pm English from October to February).

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Government of Rajasthan's official sites before you go.
Arrive at opening time to beat the heat and the crowds.
Allow 2–3 hours, and combine with Jaigarh Fort above.

places.name: Hawa Mahal
places.summary: The 'Palace of Winds': a five-storey pink facade of 953 latticed windows built in 1799 for the royal women to watch the street below.
places.seoTitle: Hawa Mahal Jaipur: History, Timings & How to Visit
places.seoDescription: Visit Hawa Mahal, Jaipur's Palace of Winds: its 953 windows, why it was built, the rear entrance and ramps inside, opening hours and nearby old-city sights.

images.alt: The pink sandstone facade of Hawa Mahal with rows of small latticed windows, Jaipur
images.caption: The facade of Hawa Mahal

overview.text:
Hawa Mahal, the 'Palace of Winds', was built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh and designed by Lal Chand Ustad. Its five-storey facade on the main street of the old city is a honeycomb of 953 small latticed windows, or jharokhas. They were designed so that the royal women, who lived in purdah, could watch everyday life and festival processions in the street below without being seen.

There is no front entrance: you go in from the back and climb ramps, not stairs, to the upper floors for the view through the windows. A small museum inside displays Rajasthani miniature art. The best view of the facade itself is from across the street.

items.title: Entrance
items.body: From the rear of the building, not the street facade.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Government of Rajasthan's official sites before you go.
Photograph the facade in the morning, when the sun lights the front.
Rooftop cafes across the street have good views of the facade.
The pink façade with 953 jharokhas, built so royal women could watch the street unseen.
The floors inside: Sharad Mandir with coloured glasswork, then Ratan, Vichitra, Prakash and Hawa Mandir.
Ramps instead of stairs, reached from the rear entrance.
A small museum of Rajasthani miniature art.

how_to_reach.text: Hawa Mahal is on the main road of the walled old city. There is no entrance from the façade side — walk round to the rear. The City Palace and Jantar Mantar are a short walk away, and the metro's Pink Line ends at Badi Chaupar in the old city.

items.body: Combine it with the City Palace and Jantar Mantar the same morning.
Shop for jewellery and textiles in Johari Bazaar.

places.name: City Palace, Jaipur
places.summary: The royal palace at the heart of the old city: courtyards, the Mubarak Mahal, the seven-storey Chandra Mahal and a museum of royal collections.
places.seoTitle: City Palace Jaipur: Timings, Tickets & What to See
places.seoDescription: Visit the City Palace in Jaipur: opening hours, standard vs Royal Splendour tickets, the Mubarak Mahal, the Chandra Mahal and the Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum.

images.alt: The cream and pink seven-storey Chandra Mahal of the City Palace in Jaipur
images.caption: Chandra Mahal, City Palace

overview.text:
Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II founded the City Palace in 1727 as part of his new city of Jaipur. Its courtyards, halls and gardens mix Rajput and Mughal architecture, and the palace is still home to Jaipur's royal family while also housing the Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum.

You enter through the Virendra Pol into the first courtyard, where the Mubarak Mahal holds part of the museum. Beyond it rises the seven-storey Chandra Mahal. A standard ticket covers its first floor; a separate 'Royal Splendour' ticket opens the private upper floors, including the blue Sukh Niwas. The palace is in the heart of the old city, about 4 km from the railway station.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: A standard ticket covers the museum and the Chandra Mahal's first floor; the 'Royal Splendour' ticket adds the upper floors. Check current prices before you go.
Mubarak Mahal in the first courtyard, now part of the museum.
The seven-storey Chandra Mahal, still partly the royal family's home.
Upper floors on the Royal Splendour ticket: the blue Sukh Niwas, the mirrored Shobha Niwas and the Mukut Niwas 'crown'.
The Teej procession, when an idol of Parvati is carried through the palace.

how_to_reach.text: The City Palace is in the heart of the old city, about 4 km from Jaipur Junction railway station. Jantar Mantar is next door and Hawa Mahal a short walk away.

items.body: Visit Govind Dev Ji, the royal family's Krishna temple in the palace grounds.
Walk next door to Jantar Mantar.

places.name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
places.summary: Jai Singh II's 18th-century observatory of 19 giant instruments, including the world's largest stone sundial — a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.seoTitle: Jantar Mantar Jaipur: Instruments, Timings & Tips
places.seoDescription: Visit Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, the UNESCO-listed observatory: the 27 m Samrat Yantra sundial, how the instruments work, opening hours and nearby sights.

images.commons: File:20191218 Brihat Samrat Yantra, Jantar Mantar, Jaipur, 0909 8993.jpg
images.alt: The curved stone walls and stairs of the giant Samrat Yantra sundial at Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
images.caption: The Vrihat Samrat Yantra

overview.text:
Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, a keen astronomer, built five observatories across India; Jaipur's, completed between 1728 and 1734, is the largest. It is a collection of 19 instruments in stone and marble for observing the positions of the sun and stars with the naked eye, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The star is the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, a 27 m sundial — the largest stone sundial in the world — whose shadow tells the time to about 2 seconds. A guide makes a big difference here: the instruments only come alive when someone explains how to read them. Jantar Mantar is right next to the City Palace and close to Hawa Mahal.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9 am – 5 pm.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Government of Rajasthan's official sites before you go.
Come on a sunny morning — the sundials need sunshine to work.
There is little shade, so bring a hat and water.
The Vrihat Samrat Yantra, a 27 m sundial accurate to about 2 seconds.
About 20 main fixed instruments for naked-eye astronomy, listed by UNESCO.
The largest of the five observatories Jai Singh II built across India.

how_to_reach.text: Jantar Mantar is next to the City Palace in the old city, a short drive or walk from Hawa Mahal. Open 9 am to 5 pm; a guided tour makes the instruments far easier to understand.

places.name: Nahargarh Fort
places.summary: The 1734 fort on the ridge above Jaipur — the city's favourite sunset viewpoint, with a sculpture park inside.
places.seoTitle: Nahargarh Fort Jaipur: Sunset Views & Visitor Guide
places.seoDescription: Visit Nahargarh Fort on the Aravalli ridge above Jaipur: its history, the Sculpture Park, panoramic city views and why it is Jaipur's best sunset spot.

images.caption: Rooftops of Nahargarh Fort

overview.text:
Nahargarh — the name means 'abode of tigers' — was built in 1734 on the Aravalli ridge that forms the northern backdrop of Jaipur, and expanded in 1868. Once part of the city's defences, today it is best known for its views: the whole of Jaipur spreads out below, with the Jal Mahal in Man Sagar Lake (which is no longer open to visitors) in the distance.

Inside the fort, the Government of Rajasthan has set up a Sculpture Park in the old palace rooms. Come in the late afternoon and stay for sunset over the city.

items.body: Go for sunset, and arrange your ride back down before dark.
Madhvendra Palace: the suite of apartments Sawai Ram Singh built for his nine queens.
The Sculpture Park, a contemporary art gallery in the old palace rooms.
The Jaipur Wax Museum, inside the fort.
Sunset over the city from the ramparts.

how_to_reach.text: Nahargarh sits on the ridge right above the old city. You can walk up the steps for free; the fort's interior needs a ticket.

items.body: Madhvendra Palace, built by Sawai Ram Singh for his nine queens.

places.name: Jaigarh Fort
places.summary: The 1726 hilltop bastion that guarded Amber Fort, home to the Jaivana cannon.
places.seoTitle: Jaigarh Fort Jaipur: Jaivana Cannon, Timings & Views
places.seoDescription: Visit Jaigarh Fort above Amber: its history as Amber's defensive bastion, the Jaivana cannon, opening hours and views over Amber Fort and Maota Lake.

images.alt: Red sandstone walls and courtyard of Jaigarh Fort on the hill above Amber
images.caption: Jaigarh Fort

overview.text:
Jaigarh Fort was commissioned in 1726 by Jai Singh II as the defensive bastion for the Amber palace complex below it, on the hill the Ministry of Tourism calls the 'Hill of Eagles'. Its long walls are visible from everywhere in Amber, and it is linked to Amber Fort by underground tunnels.

The main draw is the Jaivana cannon, which the Ministry of Tourism describes as the largest cannon on wheels. From the ramparts there are views over Amber Fort and Maota Lake.

items.body: Enter through the triple-arched Awani Darwaza.
See the Jaivana cannon — the fort was the dynasty's main cannon foundry in the Mughal era.
Walk through the Lalit Mandir, Vilas Mandir and Laxmi Vilas palaces.
Look down on Amber Fort and Maota Lake from the ramparts.

how_to_reach.text: Jaigarh is about 15 km from Jaipur on Cheelka Teela, the Hill of Eagles, directly above Amber Fort; tunnels link the two.

items.body: The Jaivana cannon, described by the Ministry of Tourism as the largest cannon on wheels.
The triple-arched Awani Darwaza and the Lalit Mandir and Vilas Mandir palaces.

places.summary: Rajasthan's oldest museum, an Indo-Saracenic landmark in Ram Niwas Garden, lit up every night.
places.seoTitle: Albert Hall Museum Jaipur: Galleries, Timings & Night View
places.seoDescription: Albert Hall Museum, Jaipur: 16 galleries and about 20,000 artefacts in an 1880s Indo-Saracenic building in Ram Niwas Garden, open into the evening.

images.alt: The domed Albert Hall Museum in Ram Niwas Garden
images.caption: Albert Hall Museum

overview.text:
The Albert Hall Museum stands in the middle of Ram Niwas Garden. Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II commissioned it in 1868 to designs by Samuel Swinton Jacob, and Maharaja Sawai Madho Singh II opened it to the public in 1887.

Its 16 galleries hold about 20,000 artefacts — miniature paintings, sculpture, textiles, arms, jewellery, a rare Persian garden carpet and an Egyptian mummy. After dark the building is lit up in colour.

items.title: Hours
items.body: 9 am – 5 pm and 7 – 9:30 pm (Incredible India)

items.title: Where
items.body: Ram Niwas Garden, which also has a bird park, a zoo and an art gallery
Come back after 7 pm to see the building lit up.

places.name: Jal Mahal
places.summary: The 'Water Palace' rising from Man Sagar Lake on the road to Amber — seen from the lakeside promenade.
places.seoTitle: Jal Mahal Jaipur: The Water Palace on Man Sagar Lake
places.seoDescription: Jal Mahal, Jaipur's Water Palace in Man Sagar Lake: its history from 1699, why four of its five storeys are under water, and where to see it.

images.alt: Jal Mahal in the middle of Man Sagar Lake
images.caption: Jal Mahal

overview.text:
Jal Mahal rises from Man Sagar Lake beside the road from Jaipur to Amber. Its foundations date from 1699; when the lake is full, the lower four of its five storeys are under water, so only the top floor shows.

The palace itself is not open to tourists. You see it from the roadside promenade on the lake's west shore, and it is lit up at night. Nearby, the royal cenotaphs at Gaitore make a quiet stop.

items.body: Stop on the way to or from Amber Fort — it is on the same road.
Come at sunset or after dark, when the palace is lit.
For the view from above, go up to Nahargarh Fort.

places.name: Galtaji
places.summary: A spring-fed temple complex in the Aravalli hills east of Jaipur, known as the Monkey Temple.
places.seoTitle: Galtaji Temple Jaipur: The Monkey Temple & Holy Kunds
places.seoDescription: Galtaji, about 10 km east of Jaipur: a pink-sandstone temple complex with seven spring-fed kunds in the Aravalli hills, busiest at Makar Sankranti.

images.commons: File:Zanana Kund Aur Galta Ji Ka Mandir - edited.jpg
images.alt: Galtaji temple and its kund in the Aravalli hills
images.caption: Galtaji

overview.text:
Galtaji is a Hindu pilgrimage site tucked into the Aravalli hills about 10 km east of Jaipur. More palace than temple in looks, the pink-sandstone complex has temples, pavilions and seven holy kunds (water tanks) fed by natural springs.

Troops of monkeys live around the complex — hence its nickname, the Monkey Temple.

items.body: Seven holy kunds, fed by water flowing from the Gaumukh, a rock shaped like a cow's head.
The Galta Kund, the most revered of them.
The spot where Tulsidas is said to have written part of the Ramcharitmanas.

how_to_reach.text: Galtaji is about 10 km east of Jaipur in the Aravalli hills; go by rickshaw, cab or car.

best_time.text: It is busiest at Makar Sankranti in January, when pilgrims come to bathe; Jaipur's cooler months make the climb easier.

items.body: Keep food out of sight — the monkeys are bold.
Dress modestly; this is an active pilgrimage site.

places.seoTitle: Birla Mandir Jaipur: Timings & What to See
places.seoDescription: Birla Mandir (Lakshmi Narayan Temple), Jaipur: a 1988 white-marble temple below Moti Dungri, with carved images, stained glass and evening lighting.

images.alt: The white-marble Birla Mandir in Jaipur
images.caption: Birla Mandir

overview.text: The Lakshmi Narayan temple — better known as Birla Mandir — was built of white marble by the Birla family in 1988 and stands at the foot of Moti Dungri. Inside are images of Vishnu and Lakshmi carved from a single marble slab, stained-glass windows showing stories of the gods, and a small museum of the Birla family's possessions.

items.body: 8 am – noon and 4 – 8 pm (Incredible India)
Visit the Moti Dungri Ganesh temple next door.
Combine with the Albert Hall Museum.

best_time.text: Come in the evening, when the temple reopens at 4 pm and its three marble domes are lit up after dark.

how_to_reach.text: It stands at the foot of Moti Dungri, next to the Ganesh temple, about 6 km from Jaipur Junction station.

places.name: Govind Dev Ji Temple
places.summary: The Jaipur royal family's Krishna temple, in the City Palace grounds.
places.seoTitle: Govind Dev Ji Temple Jaipur: History & Festivals
places.seoDescription: Govind Dev Ji Temple in Jaipur's City Palace grounds: the Krishna idol brought from Vrindavan, the record-breaking prayer hall, and Janmashtami crowds.

images.alt: Devotees at the Govind Dev Ji temple, Jaipur
images.caption: Govind Dev Ji Temple

overview.text: Govind Dev Ji stands within the City Palace grounds. It is a rare spire-less temple, and it houses the image of Krishna that Sawai Jai Singh II brought from Vrindavan; the royal family worshipped it as their own deity, and it remains one of Jaipur's most loved temples. Its prayer hall holds a Guinness record for the widest single-span RCC flat roof.

best_time.text: Janmashtami and Holi draw thousands of devotees. In the evening, a 3-D projection-mapped light and sound show at Jainiwas Udyan tells the temple's story.

items.body: Walk on into the City Palace.
Visit Jantar Mantar next door.

items.title: The idol
items.body: Hidden at Amer in Aurangzeb's reign, brought to Jaipur by Sawai Jai Singh II after 1714

items.title: Where

how_to_reach.text: It is about 6 km from Jaipur Junction railway station; the white-marble Birla Mandir stands next to it.

images.alt: The stairway climbing to Garh Ganesh temple
images.caption: Garh Ganesh Temple

overview.text: Garh Ganesh sits on an Aravalli hilltop above the city. About 365 steps — one for each day of the year — lead up to it, and the climb is rewarded with panoramic views over Jaipur.

places.name: Panna Meena ka Kund
places.summary: A geometric old stepwell in Amer town, close to Amber Fort.
places.seoTitle: Panna Meena ka Kund: Jaipur's Stepwell in Amer
places.seoDescription: Panna Meena ka Kund, the stepwell in Amer near Amber Fort: once a water source and meeting place, now one of Jaipur's most photographed spots.

images.commons: File:20191219 Panna Meena ka Kund step well, Amber, Jaipur, 1130 9630.jpg
images.alt: Criss-crossing steps of Panna Meena ka Kund
images.caption: Panna Meena ka Kund

overview.text: Panna Meena ka Kund is a centuries-old stepwell in Amer town, a short walk from Amber Fort. It was once the neighbourhood's water source and a place where people gathered to talk and escape the desert heat; today it is one of Jaipur's most photographed sights.

places.name: Gaitore
places.summary: The marble cenotaphs of Jaipur's rulers, below Nahargarh off the Amber road.
places.seoTitle: Gaitore Ki Chhatriyan: Royal Cenotaphs of Jaipur
places.seoDescription: Gaitore, Jaipur: the marble and sandstone chhatris of the Kachhwaha rulers, used as the royal cremation ground from 1733, just off the Amber road.

images.alt: Carved marble chhatris at Gaitore
images.caption: Gaitore

overview.text: Just off the Jaipur–Amber road, Gaitore holds the cenotaphs (chhatris) of Jaipur's rulers. Jai Singh II chose it as the royal cremation ground, and from 1733 each Kachhwaha ruler was cremated here; the chhatris are carved from marble and sandstone. It is close to Jal Mahal on the same road.

places.name: Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing
places.summary: A museum of block-printed textiles in a restored haveli in Amer.
places.seoTitle: Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing, Amer (Jaipur)
places.seoDescription: Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing in Amer: block-printed textiles, tools and techniques in a UNESCO-awarded restored haveli near Amber Fort.

images.alt: The restored haveli housing the Anokhi Museum
images.caption: Anokhi Museum

overview.text: A ten-minute walk through the cobbled lanes of Amer, the Anokhi Museum of Hand Printing opened in 2005 in a restored haveli. It shows block-printed textiles alongside the tools and images that explain how they are made. The restoration won a UNESCO heritage conservation award in 2000.

items.body: Combine with Amber Fort and Panna Meena ka Kund.
See block printing at its source in Bagru, 32 km from Jaipur.

places.name: Johari Bazaar
places.summary: The old city's jewellery and textile street, beside Hawa Mahal.
places.seoTitle: Johari Bazaar & Jaipur's Markets: What to Buy
places.seoDescription: Shopping in Jaipur's old city: Johari Bazaar for jewellery and textiles, Bapu Bazaar for mojaris, Rajasthali for crafts — and Sunday closures.

images.alt: Shops along Johari Bazaar in Jaipur's old city
images.caption: Johari Bazaar

overview.text: Johari Bazaar is the old city's jewellery street, also known for clothes and textiles; it runs past Hawa Mahal. Bapu Bazaar is the place for mojari shoes and textiles, and Rajasthali, the Rajasthan Government showroom on MI Road, sells crafts at fixed prices; Nehru and Tripolia bazaars and the stalls at Badi and Choti Chaupar round out the old-city shopping.

items.body: Jewellery and gems in Johari Bazaar.
Lac bangles made by Jaipur artisans.
Block-printed Sanganeri, Bagru and Dabu textiles.
Most markets are closed on Sundays.
Rajasthali on MI Road is the government showroom if you prefer fixed prices.

how_to_reach.text: Johari Bazaar runs through the walled old city past Hawa Mahal. The metro's Pink Line ends at Badi Chaupar, at the bazaar's northern end.

places.name: Isarlat (Swarg Suli)
places.summary: A 60-ft victory tower near Tripolia Gate with views over the old city.
places.seoTitle: Isarlat (Swarg Suli) Jaipur: The Victory Tower
places.seoDescription: Isarlat, or Swarg Suli: a 60-ft minaret near Tripolia Gate in Jaipur's old city, built in 1749 by Raja Ishwari Singh, with views over the city.

overview.text: Isarlat, also called Swarg Suli ('heaven-piercing minaret'), is a 60-ft tower near Tripolia Gate in the old city. Raja Ishwari Singh built it in 1749 to mark a victory, and from the top there are wide views over Jaipur. It is a short walk from the City Palace and Jantar Mantar.

places.name: Sisodia Rani Garden
places.summary: A terraced Mughal-style garden 8 km from Jaipur on the Agra road.
places.seoTitle: Sisodia Rani Garden Jaipur: Terraces & Murals
places.seoDescription: Sisodia Rani Palace and Garden, 8 km from Jaipur on the Agra road: a terraced Mughal-style garden with fountains and murals of Radha and Krishna.

overview.text: Sisodia Rani Palace and Garden lies 8 km from Jaipur on the Agra road. Laid out in Mughal style over several terraces, it has fountains, water channels and pavilions painted with the legends of Radha and Krishna. Jai Singh II built it for his Sisodia queen. Nearby, the Vidyadhar garden is named after Jaipur's chief architect.

places.name: Jhalana Leopard Safari
places.summary: Safaris in a forest on Jaipur's edge, known for leopard sightings.
places.seoTitle: Jhalana Leopard Safari Jaipur: What to Expect
places.seoDescription: Jhalana, on Jaipur's south-eastern edge: a 1,978-hectare forest whose safaris are known for leopard sightings, minutes from the city.

images.alt: Leopards in the Jhalana forest, Jaipur
images.caption: Jhalana

overview.text: Jhalana is a 1,978-hectare forest block on Jaipur's south-eastern edge. Its safaris are known for leopard sightings — unusual this close to a big city. The dry deciduous forest is good for birdwatching, and inside are a royal hunting lodge (shikar oudhi) built in 1835 and a Kali temple.

places.name: Amber Fort Sound and Light Show
places.summary: The evening son-et-lumière at Amber Fort.
places.seoTitle: Amber Fort Sound & Light Show: Timings by Season
places.seoDescription: The Amber Fort sound and light show: Rajasthan Tourism's seasonal timings for the English and Hindi shows, and what the show covers.

overview.text: Every evening Amber Fort hosts a sound and light show that tells its history through local legends and folk music, with shows in English and Hindi. Show times change with the season, so check them with Rajasthan Tourism on the day. Amber is about 11 km from the city, so plan a cab or rickshaw back after the show.

places.name: Jaipur Kite Festival
places.summary: Kite flying over the city around 14 January (Makar Sankranti).
places.seoTitle: Jaipur Kite Festival: Makar Sankranti in the Pink City
places.seoDescription: Jaipur's Kite Festival around 14 January: kites fill the sky for Makar Sankranti, with a tourism-department festival and cultural shows.

overview.text: Around 14 January — Makar Sankranti — kites fill the sky over Jaipur. The tourism department holds a kite festival with cultural performances, and Galtaji draws its biggest crowds the same day. In the evening, fireworks and lit kites brighten the skyline.

places.name: Gangaur and Teej in Jaipur
places.summary: Jaipur's two great women's festivals, with royal processions.
places.seoTitle: Gangaur & Teej in Jaipur: Festival Dates & Processions
places.seoDescription: Gangaur (Chaitra, March–April) and Teej (monsoon) in Jaipur: what they celebrate and the procession through the City Palace.

overview.text: Gangaur, one of Rajasthan's most important festivals, honours Shiva and Parvati in the Hindu month of Chaitra (March–April). Gangaur begins the day after Holi and lasts 16 days, celebrating spring, harvest and marriage. Teej marks the monsoon; in Jaipur a grand procession carries an idol of Parvati through the City Palace.

places.name: Jaipur Literature Festival
places.summary: One of the world's biggest literary festivals, every January.
places.seoTitle: Jaipur Literature Festival (JLF): When & Where
places.seoDescription: The Jaipur Literature Festival: founded in 2006, held every January, and since 2025 at Hotel Clarks Amer.

overview.text: Founded in 2006 by Namita Gokhale and William Dalrymple, the Jaipur Literature Festival is held every January — the 2020 edition ran from 23 to 27 January at Diggi Palace. Since 2025 it has been held at Hotel Clarks Amer to make room for its crowds.

places.name: Bagru
places.summary: A block-printing village 32 km from Jaipur on the Ajmer road.
places.seoTitle: Bagru Block Printing Village near Jaipur
places.seoDescription: Bagru, 32 km southwest of Jaipur: the village of hand block printing with vegetable dyes and mud-resist Dabu prints — an easy half-day trip.

images.commons: File:Woman doing Block Printing at Bagru village, Jaipur, India.jpg
images.alt: A woman block-printing cloth at Bagru
images.caption: Bagru

overview.text:
Bagru lies about 32 km southwest of Jaipur on the Ajmer road. It is known for hand block printing with natural dyes, and especially for Dabu, a mud-resist technique in which a paste of mud is printed onto the cloth to keep the dye out.

Printers use wooden blocks and colour the cloth with vegetable dyes — indigo for blue, madder root for red, turmeric for yellow — giving Bagru prints their earthy tones and floral patterns.

items.body: Watch printers and dyers at work.
See the craft's history first at the Anokhi Museum in Amer.
Continue west to Sambhar Lake in winter for flamingos.

places.name: Chand Baori (Abhaneri)
places.summary: A vast 8th–9th-century stepwell in Abhaneri village.
places.seoTitle: Chand Baori Abhaneri: India's Great Stepwell
places.seoDescription: Chand Baori in Abhaneri: an 8th–9th-century stepwell with 3,500 steps over 13 storeys and the Harshat Mata temple beside it — a day trip from Jaipur.

images.alt: The geometric steps of Chand Baori stepwell
images.caption: Chand Baori

overview.text:
Chand Baori, in Abhaneri village, is a stepwell dated to the 8th–9th century. It has 3,500 narrow steps over 13 storeys; at the bottom the air is 5–6 °C cooler than at the surface.

Beside it stands the Harshat Mata temple.

places.name: Sambhar Lake
places.summary: India's largest inland salt lake, about 70 km from Jaipur — flamingos in winter.
places.seoTitle: Sambhar Salt Lake: Flamingos & Salt Pans near Jaipur
places.seoDescription: Sambhar, India's largest inland salt lake, about 70 km from Jaipur: winter flamingos, salt pans worked for a thousand years, and when to go.

images.alt: The salt flats of Sambhar Lake
images.caption: Sambhar Lake

overview.text: Sambhar is India's largest inland salt lake, about 70 km from Jaipur. Salt has been farmed in evaporation pans east of its dam for a thousand years. In winter the lake fills with flamingos and other migratory birds.

best_time.text: Come in winter for the flamingos; summer heat reaches 45 °C.

body.intro: Jaipur's festivals are as good a reason to visit as its forts. Here is when they fall and what to expect.

sections.heading: January: kites and books
sections.text: Around 14 January (Makar Sankranti) kites fill the sky and the tourism department holds a kite festival; Galtaji is busiest that day. The Jaipur Literature Festival is also held in January, since 2025 at Hotel Clarks Amer.

sections.heading: Krishna festivals

sections.heading: Rajasthan Day

sections.text: The Anokhi Museum in Amer explains block printing; in Bagru, 32 km away, you can watch printers using vegetable dyes.

guides.title: Getting to and around Jaipur
guides.summary: Airport, trains, the metro, and distances to the sights.
guides.seoTitle: Getting Around Jaipur: Airport, Metro & Distances
guides.seoDescription: Reaching and getting around Jaipur: Sanganer airport, trains from Delhi and Agra, the Pink Line metro, and distances to Amber, Jaigarh, Galtaji and day trips.

body.intro: Jaipur is easy to reach and compact at its core; the forts and day trips need a car or rickshaw.

sections.heading: Arriving
sections.text: Jaipur International Airport is at Sanganer, about 10 km south of the centre. Jaipur is about 268 km from Delhi and 232 km from Agra by road, and has direct trains — including the Shatabdi and Rajdhani — to Delhi and other major cities.

sections.heading: In the city
sections.text: The Pink Line metro runs east–west between Mansarovar and Badi Chaupar in the old city. Hawa Mahal, the City Palace and Jantar Mantar are a short walk apart.

sections.heading: To the forts
sections.text: Amber is about 11 km away — about 20–25 minutes and 200–250 rupees by rickshaw, says Incredible India. Jaigarh is about 15 km away, above Amber. Nahargarh's steps can be climbed for free.

sections.heading: Short hops
sections.text: Galtaji is about 10 km east; Sisodia Rani Garden 8 km out on the Agra road; Moti Dungri about 6 km from Jaipur Junction.

sections.heading: Day trips
sections.text: Bagru is about 32 km southwest on the Ajmer road; Sambhar Lake about 70 km away. Hire a car for these.

guides.title: First time in Jaipur: mistakes to avoid
guides.summary: Opening hours, Sundays, heat, tickets and paperwork.
guides.seoTitle: First Time in Jaipur: Mistakes to Avoid
guides.seoDescription: Avoid the common first-timer mistakes in Jaipur: Hawa Mahal closing at 4:30, Sunday bazaars, summer heat, City Palace tickets, Jal Mahal access and e-visa timing.

body.intro: Most of Jaipur's frustrations are about timing. These are the ones that catch first-time visitors.

sections.heading: Leaving Hawa Mahal too late
sections.text: It closes at 4:30 pm, and the entrance is at the back, not on the famous façade.

sections.heading: Expecting to enter Jal Mahal
sections.text: The Water Palace is not open to tourists; you see it from the promenade — or from Nahargarh above.

sections.heading: Shopping on a Sunday
sections.text: Most bazaars are closed on Sundays.

sections.heading: The wrong City Palace ticket
sections.text: The standard ticket covers only the first floor of the Chandra Mahal; the upper rooms need the Royal Splendour ticket.

sections.heading: Underestimating the heat
sections.text: Summers are long and extremely hot; plan sights for mornings and evenings.

sections.heading: Paperwork and payments
sections.text: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days ahead. Foreign visitors can pay by UPI with the UPI One World wallet. The tourist infoline is 1800-11-1363; 112 is the emergency number.
